The Oppie carries no conventional armament, relying entirely on its working equipment and environmental systems to fulfill its mission. The tractor unit mounts a minesweeper, bulldozer, and backhoe combination for clearing debris and performing earthmoving work without crew exposure, supplemented by four manipulator arms that provide reach and grip for extracting wreckage from unstable terrain. Two sprayers dispense decontaminants or suppression agents across work areas, and four searchlights provide illumination in smoke, fog, and night conditions. Twenty tons of liquid storage accommodate decontaminants, water, or other mission-critical fluids. The tractor also carries 250 kilograms of paramedic equipment, a practical inclusion given the conditions in which salvage crews typically operate.

The Oppie's fusion powerplant provides modest cruise speed suited to deliberate recovery work rather than rapid tactical movement. Its primary limitation is operational vulnerability: the vehicle carries no defensive systems, requiring escort or protected operating environments when threats are present. The working equipment demands skilled operators, and Brown-Corning recommended specialized training for all crew assigned to the vehicle.

The Oppenheimer Hazardous Material Recovery Vehicle, universally shortened to "Oppie," was developed by Brown-Corning, Limited on Caph in direct response to the catastrophic use of thermonuclear, chemical, and biological weapons during the First Succession War. Designed to support recovery teams operating in contaminated hot zones, the Oppie is a massive 150-ton environmentally sealed crawler built to work where unprotected personnel cannot survive. The design leveraged the existing Chieftain Mobile Headquarters chassis to accelerate development and production. Its combination of environmental sealing, specialized working equipment, and cargo capacity gave salvage units a platform capable of recovering BattleMech and vehicle wreckage from areas otherwise permanently inaccessible. The Oppie quickly became one of the most recognizable non-combat vehicles of the Succession War period, valued wherever NBC contamination required sustained recovery operations.

The O-65 entered service in 2822 as the initial production variant of the Oppie family. Distinguished from the later O-66 by the absence of a fully sealed infantry bay, the O-65 instead carries 18 tons of liquid storage capacity. It was suited to recovery operations where crew remained aboard during hazardous work rather than dismounting into contaminated areas. No O-65 units are known to have survived the Succession Wars, and the design represents an early chapter in the Oppie's history rather than an ongoing operational platform.

Brown-Corning, Limited developed the Oppie in direct response to the NBC weapon use that marked the opening years of the First Succession War. Building on the proven chassis of the Chieftain Mobile Headquarters, the company produced the O-65 variant beginning in 2822 to meet immediate demand from forces engaged in cleanup operations across contaminated worlds. The O-65 lacked a sealed infantry bay, instead carrying 18 tons of liquid storage, reflecting the urgency of initial production over later refinements.

Production ended violently when a Draconis Combine raiding party struck the Brown-Corning facility on Caph. Mistaking the Oppie assembly complex for a BattleMech manufacturing facility, the raiders first deployed chemical weapons that killed the plant staff and residents of surrounding neighborhoods, then destroyed the physical facility. Without replacement production, existing Oppies declined through attrition across the subsequent decades.

The Word of Blake's interest in Caph as a Protectorate world revived both the planet and the company. Blakist forces spent two years decontaminating the Brown-Corning site and rebuilding its assembly lines, then presented Raymond Brown, a direct descendant of the company's last CEO, with the original engineering blueprints. Production resumed in 3068 as the upgraded O-66, incorporating a fully sealed infantry bay and other improvements over the original design.

The Dromedary's dune buggy derived chassis gives it the ability to traverse harsh desert terrain that would strand conventional wheeled transports. Its oversized suspension and broad wheelbase distribute the vehicle's considerable weight across loose sand and broken ground, though this capability comes at the cost of speed. A top velocity of only 32 kilometers per hour makes the Dromedary one of the slower vehicles in its class, a trade-off the designers accepted given that the treacherous terrain it regularly crosses rarely permits faster travel regardless of a vehicle's theoretical performance.

The internal combustion engine is deliberately simple, requiring minimal maintenance and allowing field repairs with basic tools. A single fuel load provides a range exceeding 2,500 kilometers, enabling the Dromedary to make extended journeys between remote settlements without refueling. The primary cargo consists of a 50-ton liquid tank capable of carrying approximately 45 kiloliters of water, supplemented by four tons of standard cargo space for spare parts and crew supplies. Defensive provisions are minimal, limited to a turret-mounted machine gun and four tons of commercial-grade armor rated at BAR 5. This protection can deflect small arms fire and deter opportunistic bandits, but offers little resistance against military-grade weapons, forcing operators to rely on armed escorts when traversing particularly dangerous routes.

The Dromedary Water Transport is a large wheeled support vehicle designed by New Vandenberg Autoworks for the Taurian Concordat during the Age of War. Introduced in 2562, the 150-ton vehicle serves as a bulk water tanker for arid Periphery worlds where reliable freshwater infrastructure does not exist. Built around a modified dune buggy chassis scaled up to commercial proportions, the Dromedary prioritizes ruggedness and simplicity over speed or sophistication. Its deliberately uncomplicated engineering has earned it a reputation as one of the most dependable civilian transports operating on the fringe of settled space, a workhorse valued precisely because it demands so little from its operators.

The standard Dromedary serves as a dedicated water hauler, ferrying bulk freshwater to communities that lack wells, rivers, or functioning purification systems. Most operate along established trade routes connecting settlements to water sources, though the vehicle's off-road capability allows it to reach sites well beyond maintained roads. Operators frequently customize their vehicles, with some installing secondary tanks for transporting specialty liquids, industrial chemicals, or refined fuels. These modifications have expanded the Dromedary's commercial appeal beyond simple water delivery, though the standard water transport configuration remains by far the most common.

New Vandenberg Autoworks created the Dromedary in 2562 to address a persistent logistics problem across the Taurian Concordat's more remote holdings. Many Periphery worlds are arid planets where surface water is scarce or nonexistent, and settlements depend entirely on water shipped in from off-world or hauled overland from distant sources. Previous attempts to establish reliable ground transport across these desert environments had failed repeatedly, with conventional tanker vehicles becoming mired in loose sand or breaking down in the punishing conditions. NVA's solution was to adapt proven dune buggy suspension technology to a large-scale commercial vehicle, creating a transport that could handle the worst terrain the Periphery had to offer.

The design proved so effective that NVA never found reason to significantly alter it. Over half a millennium of continuous production has seen only minor refinements to the basic platform, proof of how well the original engineering matched the operating environment. The Dromedary's rusted-out hulks dot trade routes across the Periphery, marking where older vehicles finally succumbed to corrosion and neglect after years of service. Despite this attrition, steady production from New Vandenberg has kept the vehicle in widespread use.

The Dromedary's most celebrated individual vehicle is the Traveling Oasis, a water hauler operating on Atreus Prime in the Taurian Concordat. Primarily tasked with delivering water to uranium miners in the Dry Gulch Wastes, the Traveling Oasis also serves double duty as a militia supply vehicle. When pirates threaten the region, the vehicle accompanies local militia forces into the desert, providing logistical support while the militia hunts down the raiders. The troops stationed with the Traveling Oasis have developed a tradition of using whatever water remains after a mission to create an improvised swimming hole, a small luxury that has made the vehicle a favorite assignment among Atreus Prime's defenders.

The Dreadnought Mk II tractor is built on a 200-ton tracked chassis with both Tech D chassis and armor construction, reinforced with eight tons of commercial grade ATC armor rated at BAR 7. This protection substantially exceeds the unmodified Elite Series 3 baseline and allows the vehicle to withstand repeated strikes from medium-class weapons. A fusion power plant provides sustainable mobility for convoy operations, drawing on the same engine to power any attached trailer modules. The tractor's primary armament mounts two Hyper-Velocity Autocannon/2s and two Extended LRM-5 launchers in the central turret, providing both close-range autocannon fire and the ability to engage threats before they reach optimal direct-fire distance. Six machine guns in front sponson mounts, coordinated by Machine Gun Arrays, provide area suppression against boarding parties and raider infantry. Advanced Fire Control governs all weapons systems.

The crew of twenty-seven is distributed across officer quarters, enlisted berths, and dedicated gunner stations. Two infantry bays carry a fifty-soldier security element for deployment at fueling stops or to repel boarders. Three steerage-class quarters accommodate fifteen additional personnel, while an onboard field kitchen allows extended operations without forward supply bases. A four-ton cargo bay at the rear, accessed through a rear door, typically carries food and medical supplies for the convoy. A three-ton lift hoist at the rear assists with cargo handling and trailer servicing during stops.

The Dreadnought Mk II Land Train is a military conversion of the Gienah-DuraPaq Elite Series 3 civilian land train, developed by Marian Arms, Inc. on Alphard for the Marian Hegemony Armed Forces. Authorized by Hegemony Armed Forces commander Michael Alexander and supervised by Marian Arms technician Proculeius Lodi, the project sought to transform the Hegemony's essential ore transport vehicles into self-defending convoy platforms capable of protecting critical supply routes without diverting dedicated combat assets to escort duty. Development began in 3072 and formal introduction was achieved in 3081. Consisting of a heavily armed tractor module and a series of interchangeable armed trailer configurations, the Mk II represents one of the Hegemony's most ambitious military engineering efforts. Only two complete trains were ever constructed, making the Dreadnought Mk II among the rarest vehicles in Periphery service.

The Dreadnought Mk II tractor serves as the armored command vehicle and primary weapons platform for each land train convoy. Each tractor operates with two to four trailer modules, with Train 838 typically running two Configuration One and two Configuration Two trailers on Alphard's ore routes, and Train 520 most commonly deploying two each of Configurations Three and Four. Trailer configurations are exchanged between specific cargo runs to suit anticipated threat profiles. The tractor crew manages all turret weapons while dedicated trailer gunners handle their respective module armament, with all gunner personnel quartered aboard the tractor itself. The infantry bays allow rapid deployment of a security element at fueling stops or to repel boarding actions along remote stretches of route.

The Marian Hegemony's overland transport network has been essential to its economy since the realm's founding, with land trains ferrying ore from Alphard's distant mining fields to Nova Roma and the industrial centers supporting Marian military power. The Gienah-DuraPaq Elite Series 3 became the standard platform for this role, and by the mid-thirty-first century the Hegemony operated substantial convoys of these vehicles across Alphard's varied terrain. As the Hegemony grew from a mining operation into a Periphery power attracting raider interest, the vulnerability of these lightly defended convoys became an increasing liability.

The Word of Blake's terrorist attacks on Nova Roma in the 3060s disrupted supply shipments and rendered several convoy routes untenable. When the Blakists returned the following year and Lugdunum became a primary target, the Hegemony found itself unable to spare military assets for convoy escort. Caesar Cassius O'Reilly's response upon assuming the throne was to appoint Proculeius Lodi of Marian Arms to develop a permanent solution, commissioning a full military conversion of the Elite Series 3 platform rather than relying on improvised escort arrangements.

Lodi's program, begun in 3072, worked closely with HAF commander Michael Alexander to develop specifications for what would become the Dreadnought Mk II. In September 3079, O'Reilly met with Lodi and Alexander in closed session, reviewed the progress of the project, and approved an ambitious upgrade to the design's defensive and offensive capabilities. O'Reilly provided a generous development budget, reflecting the strategic importance the Hegemony placed on protecting its mining infrastructure.

By the late 3070s the Mk II was undergoing field trials on Alphard, with life returning to normal in the Hegemony as the two prototype trains demonstrated the viability of the armed land train concept. Train 838 and Train 520 completed their trials and entered service in 3081. FrontierTech marketed the design as both a military asset and a commercial investment opportunity for potential outside customers, though no additional units beyond the two original trains were confirmed constructed.

The Büffel VII is a seventy-ton tracked vehicle powered by a diesel internal combustion engine, a deliberate design choice that prioritizes mechanical simplicity and ease of field maintenance over the performance characteristics of fusion alternatives. Its cruising and flanking speeds are modest by military standards, reflecting the engineering doctrine that a recovery and obstacle-clearance platform requires endurance and durability rather than maneuverability. Hull plating provides substantial protection across all facets of the vehicle, with the heaviest reinforcement concentrated at the rear where the minesweeping apparatus is mounted and where the vehicle presents its profile during sweeping operations.

The vehicle's engineering toolkit defines its operational role. Twin high-capacity lift hoists mounted in the turret can recover most disabled combat vehicles when used in conjunction with the built-in trailer connectors, making the Büffel VII a primary extraction asset for formations operating in contested terrain. A reinforced bulldozer blade at the front enables rapid clearance of rubble, collapsed structures, and other battlefield obstacles. The rear-mounted minesweeper apparatus locates and neutralizes mines and unexploded ordnance, though the system requires the vehicle to operate in reverse during deployment, a deliberate concession that keeps the most heavily armored hull section facing any incoming threats during sweeping work.

For self-defense, three machine guns split between the turret and front hull provide suppressive fire against infantry, supplemented by rear-mounted vehicle grenade launchers. A modest internal cargo bay accommodates critical supplies or repair components for supported units.

The Büffel VII Engineering Support Vehicle represents one of the oldest combat-support designs still in active service anywhere in the Inner Sphere, tracing its lineage to a pre-spaceflight era when humanity first developed equipment capable of clearing battlefields and recovering disabled war machines. Introduced in 2407 by Arcturan Arms on Arcturus, the vehicle was designed to operate in the most hazardous forward areas of any conflict, extracting disabled vehicles, clearing minefields, and removing rubble obstructions that could impede military operations. The Lyran Commonwealth Armed Forces adopted it as a standard engineering support asset, and the design proved durable enough to outlast the company that built it, the state that originally commissioned it, and most of the combat equipment it was designed to support. By the thirty-first century, examples of the Büffel VII served in planetary militias, mercenary units, and foreign militaries across the Inner Sphere.

The Büffel VII in standard configuration serves as a general-purpose engineering support asset across Lyran Commonwealth formations, mercenary commands, and foreign militaries throughout the Inner Sphere. Assigned primarily to rear-area and garrison units responsible for route clearance, obstacle removal, and vehicle recovery, the design is most common in engineering detachments and support battalions rather than front-line combat elements. The vehicle's long service life and wide distribution mean it appears across a broad range of faction affiliations and unit quality levels, from well-maintained regimental assets to barely operational garrison holdovers. Operations typically pair the Büffel VII with infantry security elements to compensate for its modest self-defense capability during extended engineering work.

The Büffel VII entered Lyran Commonwealth service in 2407, produced at Arcturan Arms' facility on Arcturus to address a persistent need for a purpose-built heavy engineering vehicle capable of working under fire. The design was adopted broadly across the Lyran Commonwealth Armed Forces and spread simultaneously into civilian and industrial sectors, where its ability to clear difficult terrain and recover heavy equipment found natural application well beyond the battlefield. The Büffel VII became a fixture across Lyran military formations at every level, from the elite Guards regiments to the smallest planetary garrison commands.

The early 2540s brought a change in ownership when MacEnroe Motors acquired Arcturan Arms and assumed control of the Arcturus production line. Under MacEnroe's management, the facility introduced the Reverse Büffel variant, which swapped the positions of the minesweeper and bulldozer systems to allow mine-clearance operations at normal forward travel speed. Production at Arcturus ceased around 2551, and for the next five centuries the Büffel VII survived primarily through the vast numbers already in service. As examples passed between units, factions, and generations throughout the Succession Wars, many were operated under local designations while retaining the original specifications, and the common aftermarket practice of removing the rear grenade launchers in favor of additional cargo space further diversified the population in service.

The Büffel VII's longevity rested heavily on its diesel powerplant. An internal combustion engine required none of the specialized maintenance infrastructure that fusion-powered vehicles demanded, making the design practical for formations with limited technical resources. By the time of the Jihad, Büffel VIIs that had been in continuous service for a century or more were not unusual, maintained through locally fabricated replacement components. The design's broad presence in mercenary commands and foreign militaries reflected not only the scale of original production but the ease with which surviving units could be kept operational without specialized support.

Production resumed around 3074 when the Arcturus facility began manufacturing new Büffel VIIs under an unknown operator, coinciding with the simultaneous introduction of the related Büffel VIII series at Halfway. This renewed production reflected continued demand for battlefield engineering support across the contested frontiers of the late thirty-first century.

Built around a Class 265 internal combustion engine, the Air Car achieves an impressive top speed of roughly one hundred eighty-three kilometers per hour on its hover skirt. This makes it one of the faster ground vehicles available for civilian purchase, capable of outrunning most military vehicles over open terrain. The reliance on an ICE powerplant rather than a fusion engine keeps both purchase price and maintenance costs low, a key consideration for a vehicle intended for the civilian market. Fuel consumption is manageable for routine transit operations, though sustained high-speed travel reduces operational range considerably.

At forty tons, the Air Car carries only two tons of standard armor plating, providing minimal protection against small arms fire and little else. The vehicle mounts no weapons of any kind, leaving it entirely dependent on escort or evasion for survival in hostile environments. Despite being categorized as a transport vehicle, the Air Car lacks dedicated cargo capacity in its standard configuration, with interior volume devoted almost entirely to passenger seating and the powerplant. This limitation restricts its military utility to personnel movement rather than supply transport, a shortcoming that has led many garrison commands to prefer purpose-built military transports when available.

The Air Car is a ubiquitous civilian hovercraft found across the Inner Sphere, Periphery, and Clan occupation zones alike. Produced by countless manufacturers on hundreds of worlds, the design is a broad class of medium-weight hover transports in the thirty to fifty ton range rather than a single specific model from one factory. Intended primarily for civilian passenger and light cargo movement, the Air Car's combination of high speed, simple construction, and low operating costs has made it one of the most common ground vehicles encountered on developed worlds. Its widespread availability and ease of maintenance have also led to its frequent conscription into militia and paramilitary service, where it fills rear-area transport and courier roles despite never having been designed for the battlefield.

The base Air Car configuration sees service in virtually every military and paramilitary organization across known space, though rarely in frontline combat roles. Planetary militia forces and rear-echelon commands are the most common operators, using the vehicle for rapid personnel shuttling between installations, courier duties, and emergency evacuation runs. Mercenary commands operating on tight budgets have been known to press Air Cars into service as improvised scout vehicles, relying on their considerable speed to compensate for the complete lack of armament or meaningful protection.

The Air Car belongs to a class of civilian hover transports whose origins predate any single traceable manufacturer or production line. Vehicles fitting the Air Car's general description have been a staple of planetary transportation networks since long before the fall of the Star League, with dozens of companies across every Successor State producing their own regional variants under various trade names. The commonality of the underlying hover technology and powerplant design means that most versions are broadly interchangeable in terms of performance and handling, leading to the generic classification rather than attribution to any single manufacturer.

The Succession Wars did little to diminish Air Car availability, as the vehicle's simple construction and reliance on internal combustion technology placed it well within the manufacturing capabilities of even LosTech-era industrial bases. Where fusion-powered military vehicles became increasingly difficult to produce and maintain, ICE-driven civilian hover transports remained in steady production on virtually every inhabited world with basic manufacturing infrastructure. This durability of the supply chain ensured that Air Cars remained plentiful even during the darkest years of the Third Succession War.

Military adoption of the Air Car has always been a matter of necessity rather than preference. Garrison forces and planetary militia commands frequently requisition civilian hover transports to supplement their organic vehicle pools, particularly on worlds where purpose-built military equipment is scarce. The vehicle's high speed provides some tactical value for courier and liaison duties, but its complete lack of armament and negligible armor protection render it a liability in any engagement. Numerous after-action reports across multiple conflicts document Air Cars being destroyed in ambushes or caught in crossfire while performing rear-area transport missions, emphasizing the risks inherent in fielding civilian vehicles in combat zones.

The Air Car continues to see universal service across all major factions and eras, its role unchanged by the technological advances and political upheavals that have reshaped the Inner Sphere. From Clan occupation zones to the most remote Periphery worlds, the vehicle remains a fixture of daily civilian life and an expedient, if reluctant, addition to military motor pools.

The Silverback retains the Silverfin's 40-ton hydrofoil hull, 17-ton ICE powerplant, and Windancer Lightwave armor unchanged. Flank speed remains 120 km/h and the polymer composite foils carry over without modification. Fuel capacity increases by half a ton over the base Silverfin, extending operational range to approximately 2,352 km.

Armament shifts from the Silverfin's torpedo-machine gun combination to three machine guns in the forward turret, all guided by an Advanced Fire Control system. The elimination of the torpedo launchers was a deliberate trade, freeing tonnage for the Silverback's defining upgrade: a Guardian ECM Suite weighing 1.5 tons. The Guardian system disrupts enemy targeting and guidance systems across a meaningful area, making the Silverback particularly valuable when stationed alongside slower, better-armed flagships.

The armor protection remains identical to the base Silverfin (one ton of BAR 7 Windancer Lightwave commercial plating) meaning the Silverback is no more survivable in direct combat than the vessel it was built from. It must rely on its ECM disruption and hydrofoil speed to avoid being hit. The HUNTER communications electronics are likewise inherited unchanged and retain the same fifty-year overhaul requirement.

The Silverback Coastal Cutter is a Lyran Alliance field modification of the ancient Silverfin, introduced in 3058 as a dedicated electronic warfare escort for high-value wet navy assets. Blue water navies in the Lyran Alliance Armed Forces developed the conversion informally, stripping the torpedo launchers in favor of a Guardian ECM Suite and additional machine guns. The resulting vessel proved immediately popular among planetary militia navies looking to extend their limited capital-ship complements with electronic protection rather than direct firepower.

Where the Silverfin is a patrol tool of broad applicability, the Silverback fills a narrower and more specific role: keeping enemy targeting solutions away from Lyran naval flagships. Its recognition in LAAF wet navy records formalized what had begun as a local adaptation, and the design spread quickly through Alliance coastal forces.

The Silverback serves exclusively within Lyran Alliance wet navy forces, deployed as an electronic warfare screen for high-value naval vessels such as Jormungand-class cruisers. Typical doctrine pairs multiple Silverbacks in close escort of a flagship, providing overlapping ECM coverage to deny enemy guided-weapon solutions. The design is unsuited to independent patrol or sustained combat and depends on proximity to better-armored assets for operational effectiveness.

The Blue Hole Navy maintains a standing complement of at least three Silverbacks on permanent assignment to the BHS Brynhild, an arrangement widely cited within Alliance naval commands as a cost-effective approach to flagship protection. Other Lyran planetary militia navies have replicated this pattern to varying degrees depending on local resources and the perceived threat environment.

The Silverback emerged not from a formal development program but from ad hoc modifications carried out by Lyran Alliance coastal naval technicians in the years following the Clan Invasion. The appearance of Clan naval assets and improved guided-weapon systems made electronic warfare protection increasingly critical for Lyran surface fleets, whose aging capital ships could not easily absorb direct hits from advanced munitions. Technicians found that the Silverfin's cargo and torpedo space was sufficient to house a Guardian ECM Suite with room left for additional machine guns, and the hydrofoil hull's proven reliability made the modification straightforward to execute in field conditions.

The conversion proved popular enough to earn formal LAAF recognition by 3058, and the designation Silverback was entered into Lyran Alliance wet navy rolls as a distinct variant. Planetary militia navies throughout the Alliance quickly adopted the pattern, as it offered a way to extend the protective umbrella of limited capital ship complements without requiring new construction. Critical acclaim for the design spread through Lyran naval circles following the Blue Hole Navy's deployment of three Silverbacks as a permanent escort force for the BHS Brynhild, the planet's sole Jormungand-class cruiser. The Blue Hole arrangement became an informal model referenced by other planetary commands seeking to protect high-value vessels with minimal resources.

The Jonah is an ultra-light submersible weighing two thousand kilograms, driven by a fusion drive that delivers moderate underwater speed. A cruise pace of four and a flank pace of six are adequate for navigating deep-ocean environments without excessive energy consumption. The hull is rated to withstand depths exceeding ten kilometers, well beyond the operational envelope of most comparable craft. Armor protection is minimal, using a BAR 3 construction rating that prioritizes pressure resistance over combat survivability. The Jonah carries no weapons of any kind.

Standard equipment includes a forward-mounted searchlight, twin manipulator arms at the bow for sample collection and site work, and a rear-mounted remote sensor dispenser. Crew complement is one operator with two passenger positions, giving the vessel a total capacity of three personnel. Life-support systems are rated for continuous dives exceeding ten days without resupply.

The design's chief weaknesses are its absence of defensive armament and its classification as an obsolete, non-standard design throughout much of its operational life. Sourcing replacement components requires custom fabrication or dedicated supply chains. Cargo capacity is limited to under two hundred kilograms, constraining the volume of samples or equipment the sub can carry on a single mission. These limitations narrow the Jonah's appeal to well-supported organizations with established logistics networks.

The Jonah JN-002 is a miniaturized submersible designed for deep-water exploration and research in extreme liquid environments. Its origins trace to Ryan Systemics, an oceanographic research subsidiary of the Ryan Cartel, which had specialized in water-world environmental analysis for decades. When the Cartel's financial troubles triggered a liquidation cascade, the working prototype of a new deep-water submarine was nearly lost. The survival of that design, and its eventual transformation into the production Jonah, represents one of the more unlikely industrial recoveries in the Periphery's civilian technology sector. Introduced in 2714 on the oceanic world of Blue Hole, the Jonah carved out a niche market among deep-sea research organizations and resource extraction operations working in environments hostile to standard marine craft. Though never produced in large numbers, the design proved remarkably well-suited to its intended mission.

The JN-002 is manufactured at the Interstellar Expeditions facility on Blue Hole and distributed exclusively to IE member organizations. Its missions center on deep-ocean scientific investigation, underwater resource surveys, and environmental monitoring in liquid environments beyond the reach of surface or near-surface craft. The Jonah has seen deployment across Periphery water worlds where IE-sponsored expeditions regularly operate under conditions requiring sustained deep-dive capability. Its manipulator arms and remote sensor systems make it particularly suited for sample collection and site documentation. Operators outside IE-affiliated networks face significant logistical challenges in sourcing replacement components, effectively limiting the design to well-supplied organizational fleets with dedicated support infrastructure.

Ryan Systemics began as the environmental science arm of the Ryan Cartel, tasked with studying water-world ecosystems and developing filtration technologies for colonial water supplies. As new filtration methods undercut the Cartel's broader profits, Ryan Cartel began liquidating subsidiaries, and Systemics faced dissolution. A working prototype submarine, informally called the Jarvis, had just completed qualification trials when the liquidation began. Trevor Stefanis, a Systemics employee, managed to remove the prototype before the facilities were foreclosed, preserving the only working example of what would eventually become the Jonah.

Decades later, Trevor's great-grandson Unger Stefanis brought the dormant Jarvis design to Napa Tidal Research on Blue Hole in 2714. Pairing with Branson United to establish a manufacturing line, the venture faced immediate production constraints: a single assembly line required eight months to build each vehicle. Despite this bottleneck, sales outpaced production throughout the partnership's existence. The NTR-BU venture collapsed within a decade, around 2724, and the factory fell silent for more than three centuries. The Jonah acquired its obsolete designation during this long dormancy, and surviving units grew increasingly difficult to maintain as original components aged out of any supply chain.

In 3032, Interstellar Expeditions acquired the derelict factory site on Blue Hole. Restoration took fifteen years and over 1.6 billion Kroner, but by the mid-3040s the plant was again producing Jonahs, this time exclusively for IE member corporations. The revival coincided with renewed interstellar exploration activity across the Periphery, and the Jonah found a second generation of customers among teams investigating deep-ocean worlds and resource-rich aquatic environments. During this same period, Unger Stefanis had leveraged the Cokery Isles chain near Blue Hole as a testing ground for underwater purification infrastructure, establishing Blue Hole Bottling and reshaping the local planetary economy in the process.

The Atlantia is built around a high-strength polymer hull with equally resilient decking and paneling, designed to handle Oriente's harsh equatorial storms without compromising passenger comfort. Many buyers opt for Oriente caoba timber overlays on the decking and interior panels, providing a warm aesthetic without sacrificing structural strength. At 190 tons, the vessel achieves a top speed of approximately 55 kilometers per hour under standard configuration, with sustained cruising at just over 30 kph. BAR 3 protection is distributed across all facings, with the heaviest concentration forward where storm and wave impact is greatest.

The standard powerplant is an internal combustion engine providing a range of 1,153 kilometers on a full fuel load, sufficient for extended coastal and archipelago cruising. Hamilton Consortium offers fusion powerplant alternatives at significant additional cost, and enhanced-engine planing-hull configurations have demonstrated speeds exceeding 100 kph in private commission builds. The vessel carries nine crew in addition to seven luxury passenger berths, with custom orders able to adjust these capacities in exchange for speed or range. The bridge is outfitted with satellite navigation and communications equipment keeping the vessel connected regardless of location. Optional appointments include top-deck jacuzzis, fishing decks, a sliding roof over the dining salon, and exterior trim packages.

The Atlantia Luxury Yacht is a prestige naval vessel produced by the Hamilton Consortium on Oriente for the high-end leisure market of the Free Worlds League. Introduced in 2890 during the Late Succession Wars, the design was aimed at the wealthy civilians and merchant class who continued to prize luxury and exclusivity even during a period of broader interstellar conflict. Each thirty-meter vessel is built to order from a core design schematic, with the construction fee of 575,000 C-bills covering the development of unique custom features for every hull, meaning no two Atlantias are exactly alike. A two-year waiting period from order to delivery became a hallmark of the line, reinforcing its status as a symbol of affluence throughout the League and in export markets beyond it.

The Atlantia is deployed almost exclusively by private civilian owners throughout the Free Worlds League and export markets. Its Equipment Rating of D/X-D-C reflects its open civilian availability, practically constrained by cost and the two-year order queue. The vessel serves as a private yacht, corporate transport, and executive retreat platform for the League's wealthiest citizens. A small number of fusion-powered configurations have been built for buyers requiring higher performance. No formal military applications are on record, though the vessel's communications suite and extended range make it a practical courier or liaison platform in permissive environments. Production has continued through multiple political transitions on Oriente, remaining active under Free Worlds League, Duchy of Oriente, and Oriente Protectorate oversight before returning to FWL control in the ilClan era.

The Hamilton Consortium developed the Atlantia series in 2890 to serve the wealthy civilian market that persisted through the Late Succession Wars on Oriente and across the broader Free Worlds League. The design filled a gap for buyers who wanted a vessel that combined genuine seagoing capability with the luxury appointments expected by affluent clients, and the built-to-order production model ensured that exclusivity was baked into every hull from the outset. The combination of the 575,000 C-bill construction fee and the two-year waiting period transformed ownership of an Atlantia into a visible marker of status among League nobility and the merchant class.

Export contracts extended the Atlantia's reach beyond the League, and Hamilton steadily built a reputation for delivering resilient, well-appointed vessels that could handle Oriente's demanding equatorial conditions. The line gained broader recognition in 3065 when a custom high-performance variant built for media mogul Elliot Ikegami competed in the Halberstan endurance race on New Olympia. Ikegami placed third, but his vessel's demonstrated capability at over 100 kph drew considerable attention to the platform's engineering flexibility and generated a new wave of orders for the Consortium.

Production on Oriente continued through the Jihad and into the Dark Age, persisting under Duchy of Oriente ownership during the early Republic period before transitioning to Oriente Protectorate oversight through the DA-LR, DA-1, and DA-2 eras. The MUPL corrections log flags DA-2 Protectorate ownership as potentially suspect, noting that the Oriente Protectorate formally ended in 3139 while some records still reflect Protectorate control at the 3145 snapshot. The factory returned to Free Worlds League control by the ilClan era. Throughout these political transitions, the built-to-order civilian production model kept the line active and the Hamilton Consortium's order books filled.

The prototype Lexan weighs fifteen tons and retains the Series II's fusion engine, giving it unlimited range at speeds approaching 230 kilometers per hour. An Angel ECM suite provides electronic protection, while a recon camera serves as the primary sensor package. Two small lasers offer minimal self-defense capability, though the aircraft lacks any fire control system to employ them effectively. BAR 10 commercial armor inherited from the civilian airframe provides the only physical protection.

The production model increases mass to seventeen tons and replaces the experimental Angel ECM with a more reliable Guardian ECM suite paired with a Xilex 12 Wireless communications system. Top speed drops to 194 kilometers per hour, but the aircraft gains significant improvements. An Omni Generation Five fusion engine provides power, while Longanecker E-Series armor replaces the commercial plating. Two Defiance B3S small lasers mounted alongside a recon camera in a chin turret provide observation and self-defense capability. The production Lexan uses composite rotor materials and advanced fabrication techniques that reduce audible emissions by fifty percent over the Oceanic series. A Suresight camera system gives the operator four configurable displays capable of detecting targets at eighteen kilometers, with indirect LRM targeting telemetry available through a software bypass that voids the warranty.

The Lexan Surveillance Helo is a militarized derivative of the Oceanic Series II personal VTOL, developed by Lockheed/CBM Corporation at their Furillo plant. Originally conceived as a reconnaissance platform for the experimental Cloud Ten airship carrier, the design evolved from a limited-run prototype into a full production surveillance aircraft.

The prototype first flew in 3076 as an experimental refit of the civilian Series II airframe, incorporating military-grade electronics and light weaponry. The production model, redesigned and introduced in 3080, addressed the prototype's shortcomings while retaining the core surveillance mission. Heavier and more capable than its predecessor, the production Lexan found a receptive market among Lyran Commonwealth planetary militias, law enforcement agencies, and paramilitary organizations seeking an affordable reconnaissance platform.

The production Lexan Surveillance VTOL has become a fixture of Lyran Commonwealth planetary militias, with notable concentrations in the Timbuktu Theater, Melissia Theater, Coventry Province, and Arc-Royal Province. Law enforcement agencies and paramilitary organizations have also adopted the aircraft in significant numbers. Lockheed/CBM has aggressively marketed the design through multi-unit discounts, reduced-price upgrades, and other incentives to bolster sales. Despite commercial success in non-military markets, the LCAF has declined to adopt the Lexan for frontline service, reportedly due to its lack of a dedicated targeting and tracking system.

The Lexan Surveillance Helo traces its origins to the Cloud Nine airship disaster of 3065, which silenced interest in airship-based fighter carriers for nearly a decade. In 3074, Rebecca Cardinali, engineering director for Lockheed/CBM's personal VTOL division, attended the fifty-seventh annual EECEIECE conference. There she met Joseph Akron, cousin to Count Douglas Fassei of Cal-Boeing. A late-night debate fueled by several bottles of wine produced an unlikely collaboration when the two engineers argued over whether the Cloud Nine could have been a viable carrier platform.

Two months later, in September 3074, Cardinali presented the Lockheed/CBM regional board of directors with plans for a militarized version of the Lexan Oceanic Series II. The board approved the project immediately, granting Cardinali an expanded staff and budget with the caveat that sixteen functional prototypes be delivered by October 3075. The tight timeline forced compromises. Planned stealth armor was sacrificed for a prototype Angel ECM suite, and an ER small laser was replaced with standard small lasers lacking fire control. Meanwhile, Akron convinced his uncle to finance a new airship carrier, the Cloud Ten, as a demonstration platform.

Six prototype Lexans entered field trials with the Cloud Ten in January 3076, touring remote Lyran Alliance worlds to test surveillance and information-gathering capabilities. The prototype's Angel ECM proved expensive and its lack of proper fire control limited operational flexibility, prompting Lockheed/CBM to develop a redesigned production variant. Company executives embraced a cost-reduction philosophy, dropping the Angel ECM for the proven Guardian suite and adding a proper chin turret with integrated weapons and camera. The revamped aircraft entered production in 3080 and quickly attracted orders from law enforcement, paramilitary groups, and planetary militia commands throughout the Lyran Commonwealth.

The Strike Falcon is a 30-ton medium VTOL built around an internal combustion engine, delivering a cruise speed of approximately 119 km/h and a flank speed of 186 km/h. Its primary offensive systems are a pair of SRM 4 launchers mounted in the nose, providing effective short-range fire against armored targets. Three machine guns, positioned in the chin and on both flanks, offer broad-arc anti-infantry suppression. An Advanced Fire Control system improves crew accuracy, partially compensating for the vehicle's relatively modest armament compared to heavier dedicated gunships.

The aircraft's most operationally significant feature is its large troop bay, designed to carry one fully equipped heavy infantry platoon, or two light platoons in cramped conditions, through three access doors on the right, left, and rear. The wings serve a secondary aerodynamic function, contributing significant lift in forward flight and extending the operational radius to well over 1,500 kilometers. BAR 7 armor provides adequate protection against small arms and light weapons common to the period, but leaves the vehicle dangerously exposed to any concentrated anti-armor fire. The Easy to Pilot design quirk made the Strike Falcon accessible to a broad pool of trained crews, an important advantage when qualified rotary-wing pilots were in short supply across the Confederation's expanding military.

The Strike Falcon Attack VTOL was developed by Grand Union Battle Works on Tikonov, entering service in 2371 as the Capellan Confederation's answer to the aging OT-22 Bird of Prey rotary-wing platform. Designed to fill a demanding dual role, the Strike Falcon combined heavy infantry transport capacity with substantial fire support capability, making it one of the more versatile VTOL designs of the Age of War. Its introduction was enthusiastically received by Capellan commanders, who found its combination of speed, range, and cargo capacity well suited to the mobile warfare of the era.

The design's reputation spread quickly beyond Capellan borders, and multiple powers attempted to replicate its performance with varying degrees of success. Despite its eventual obsolescence, the Strike Falcon remained in frontline service for over a century before giving way to lighter, faster, and better-protected successors.

The Strike Falcon served across Capellan Confederation ground forces as an assault transport and fire support asset throughout the Age of War. Commanders typically deployed pairs or flights of three to insert a company-sized infantry element, with the aircraft transitioning to suppression and covering fire after troops cleared the landing zone. The design saw action along multiple contested borders, operating in coordination with ground mechanized units to exploit breakthrough opportunities and secure objectives ahead of slower-moving armor.

As the design aged into the mid-twenty-fourth century, Strike Falcons increasingly appeared in reserve and militia formations, replaced in frontline roles by more capable platforms. Following the 2510 obsolescence declaration, units transferred to civilian operators retained their transport capacity but were stripped of weapons and combat sensors.

The helicopter's place on the battlefield was never seriously in doubt during the Age of War. When the Capellan Confederation coalesced from a collection of smaller states in 2367, Tikonov contributed not just territory but a robust defense industrial base centered on Grand Union Battle Works. The OT-22 Bird of Prey had been the backbone of Tikonov's rotary-wing forces, but it was approaching the end of its service life. Grand Union Battle Works received the commission to develop a capable successor that could meet the Confederation's demands for combined-arms flexibility.

The Strike Falcon entered service in 2371 and quickly earned a strong operational reputation in Capellan formations. Its ability to insert infantry directly into contested areas, then remain on station to provide immediate fire support, made it a preferred tool for battalion and regiment commanders throughout the Age of War. Few opponents could take one down with a single hit in its heyday, and the design's durability drew attention across the Inner Sphere. Several rival powers and independent manufacturers produced copies or near-copies of the Strike Falcon during the mid-twenty-fourth century, though results were mixed.

The aircraft's shortcomings grew more pronounced as the era progressed. Advances in weapons and armor technology increasingly outpaced the Strike Falcon's protection levels, and newer platforms offered better performance across every mission parameter. By 2510, Grand Union Battle Works officially declared the design obsolete. Surviving airframes were stripped of their combat systems and transitioned to civilian cargo and passenger roles, where some remained in operation for decades after military retirement.

The Grand Union Battle Works facility on Tikonov continued operating through subsequent centuries under shifting ownership. Tikonov's contested position in Inner Sphere politics brought the world through Capellan Confederation, Tikonov Free Republic, and Federated Commonwealth control during the Succession Wars and Clan Invasion eras, before returning to Capellan hands during the Civil War period. The planet later passed through independent administration, Republic of the Sphere stewardship, a brief Federated Suns interval, and ultimately back to the Confederation during the ilClan era. The factory itself, long since repurposed from Strike Falcon production, reflects that turbulent history of planetary control.

The Sturmvogel Gunship shares its power plant with the Maritime Patrol variant, reaching a maximum speed above 120 kilometers per hour with an unlimited patrol range. The primary difference lies in its armament. Rather than the rotary autocannon of the standard design, the Gunship mounts a light Gauss rifle, providing greater reach and accuracy at the cost of the burst-fire volume that makes the Maritime Patrol effective at close engagement ranges. Three mine dispensers remain for area-denial, though one fewer than the standard model reduces flexibility when laying barrier fields.

The Gunship's most pronounced weakness is its armor, which falls short even of the Maritime Patrol's already thin protection. This deficiency was the central reason LAAF evaluators rejected the design for front-line combat service. Crews compensate through the same high-speed, terrain-exploiting tactics used by Maritime Patrol crews, keeping the craft at stand-off range and avoiding direct engagement with armored opponents. For operators willing to accept the survivability trade-off, the light Gauss rifle provides a genuine long-range capability that the rotary autocannon cannot duplicate, giving the Gunship a distinct role when used in conjunction with better-protected patrol craft.

The Sturmvogel Gunship is the original military prototype that preceded the more widely known Maritime Patrol variant. Developed by Nashan Diversified on Furillo in 3059, the design emerged from an attempt to build a Lyran combat WiGE with meaningful offensive reach. Though rejected by Lyran Alliance Armed Forces evaluators for insufficient armor protection, the Gunship established the speed, power plant, and modular foundation that the Maritime Patrol design built upon. Small numbers entered service with Lyran militia and planetary defense forces who valued its firepower over its survivability, and the design has remained available from Nashan's Furillo facility despite never achieving the widespread adoption of its better-known sibling.

The Sturmvogel Gunship is deployed as a fire support and interdiction asset in units lacking access to heavier WiGE combat vehicles. The light Gauss rifle gives it a stand-off advantage over the standard Maritime Patrol model, making it useful for harassing incoming waterborne forces and supporting other patrol craft from a distance. Mine dispensers provide secondary area-denial capability. Commanders typically hold the Gunship behind the engagement line, using faster and better-armed surface assets to screen it while it engages at range. Independent operations against armored opposition without support are strongly discouraged given the design's vulnerability to return fire.

Nashan Diversified began development of what would become the Sturmvogel line in the late 3050s, following the Lyran Alliance's secession from the Federated Commonwealth in 3058. With access to Federated Suns-built patrol WiGEs growing uncertain, Nashan's designers set out to produce a Lyran-built replacement with genuine combat capability. The company's Furillo facility, already experienced in vehicle construction, was tasked with delivering a WiGE gunship that could compete with existing patrol craft in both speed and firepower.

The resulting prototype, completed in 3059, carried a light Gauss rifle and mine dispensers on a high-speed WiGE hull. LAAF evaluators were impressed by the weapon fit but concluded the armor protection was inadequate for any role involving direct engagement with enemy combat vehicles. The rejection pushed Nashan to pivot the design toward coast guard and militia markets, producing the Maritime Patrol variant with a rotary autocannon and search-and-rescue equipment in its place. The Maritime Patrol eclipsed the Gunship commercially, but Nashan continued to offer the Gunship configuration for customers who prioritized stand-off firepower over versatility.

The Gunship found a modest market among militia commanders defending contested coastlines who needed reach that the standard model's rotary autocannon could not provide. Production at Furillo continued alongside the Maritime Patrol line through the Civil War, the Jihad, and into the Dark Age, though the Gunship always remained the rarer of the two designs.

As a trailer unit, the TGV Omni Railcar carries no engine of its own and relies entirely on one or more Adelante tractors for motive power. Its fifteen-and-a-half-ton chassis supports one hundred and one and a half tons of reconfigurable pod space distributed across seventeen equipment slots, providing exceptional payload flexibility for its weight class. BAR 9 armor offers better ballistic protection than the tractor itself, a design choice reflecting the trailer's role as the system's primary payload carrier where passengers, cargo, or military assets require shielding from hostile fire.

The omni-pod system represents the core innovation of the entire Adelante platform. Overhead magnetic cranes at equipped depots can lift entire configuration modules out of the trailer's open-topped chassis channel and replace them within minutes, even while passengers remain aboard adjacent cars in the same train consist. This allows operators to adjust train composition on short notice, switching between luxury passenger service and bulk cargo hauling without taking vehicles out of the operational rotation. The design carries the Difficult to Maintain quirk, however, reflecting the complexity of its omni-pod interfaces and the specialized depot equipment required for configuration changes. Facilities lacking the proper magnetic crane infrastructure cannot perform field swaps, limiting operational flexibility away from established rail corridors.

The TGV Omni Railcar is a one-hundred-twenty-ton modular trailer designed by Alstom Rail Corporation in partnership with Blackwell Corporation during the early 3060s. Created as the interchangeable payload component of the Adelante rail system, the TGV uses omni-technology to allow rapid reconfiguration between five standard pod layouts covering passenger transport, cargo hauling, and military support roles. Swapping configurations requires only a concrete service channel equipped with overhead magnetic cranes, a process completed in minutes rather than the hours demanded by traditional railcar maintenance. This flexibility made the TGV platform commercially attractive to both civilian transport operators and military logistics commands, with universal availability ensuring broad distribution across the Inner Sphere.

Configuration A maximizes passenger capacity with ten second-class quarters and six steerage quarters, plus one and a half tons of cargo space. This mass-transit layout carries the highest passenger count of any TGV configuration, serving commuter corridors and high-volume intercity routes where affordable transportation takes priority over individual comfort.

The TGV Omni Railcar entered service shortly after the Adelante tractor in the early 3060s as the payload component of Alstom Rail Corporation's modular rail system. Where conventional railcar operations required time-consuming switchyard procedures to reorganize train composition, the TGV's omni-pod design allowed complete reconfiguration at any depot equipped with the standardized magnetic crane channels. This capability proved commercially transformative, enabling operators to run morning passenger express services and afternoon freight hauls using the same trailer frames.

Military adoption followed quickly after the FedCom Civil War demonstrated the system's tactical potential on New Avalon. The Davion Heavy Guards configured TGV trailers for battle armor and hovercraft transport, while a dedicated command variant provided mobile headquarters capability across the planet's rail network. These improvised military applications led Alstom to formalize military-specific configurations, including the dedicated Military Support and MASH layouts that supplemented the original civilian passenger and cargo designs.

The platform's universal availability designation reflects its broad commercial distribution rather than any specific factional adoption. Rail infrastructure varies enormously between worlds, and the TGV system requires both compatible track gauges and depot facilities equipped with the specialized magnetic crane channels. Worlds with extensive rail networks have adopted the system enthusiastically, while those lacking the infrastructure investment find the platform impractical regardless of the trailer's technical merits. Production has continued steadily through the Jihad era and into the Dark Age, with the system's civilian utility ensuring demand even during periods of reduced military procurement.
